title: High Availability and Resilience knowledge check

questions.prompt: Which topic is explicitly covered in “High Availability and Resilience”?
options: A production task outside the lesson scope
questions.explanation: The supplied Linux.pdf lists “Redundant services” under lesson 235, “High Availability and Resilience”. The practical point is to connect the syllabus term with an observable Linux workflow.

questions.prompt: Which is the safest default for practising high availability and resilience?
options: Run the first command found online with administrator privileges on a production system.
Assume every Linux distribution ships the same tools and default configuration.
Skip verification because the example produced output once.
Use a controlled Linux VM or disposable test directory, inspect the result, and record the distribution/version assumptions.
questions.answer_key: Use a controlled Linux VM or disposable test directory, inspect the result, and record the distribution/version assumptions.
questions.explanation: For High Availability and Resilience, use a controlled lab, change one factor at a time, and record the exact result. Some operations in this area can affect data, availability, or access if performed on a real system.

questions.prompt: What is the strongest verification approach after a change or observation related to high availability and resilience?
options: Reproduce the observation, test one boundary or failure case, compare expected and actual results, and document the relevant version or distribution.
Change several unrelated settings at once and infer which one fixed the problem.
Treat a missing command as proof that Linux is not installed.
Hide the error output and record only the final screen.
questions.answer_key: Reproduce the observation, test one boundary or failure case, compare expected and actual results, and document the relevant version or distribution.
questions.explanation: Repeatable evidence and a boundary case are more informative than a single successful run. Document command versions, distribution-specific behavior, and any limitation.
